Persistent HIV-1 replication maintains the tissue reservoir during therapy
Here we show that virus evolution and trafficking between tissue compartments continues in patients with undetectable levels of virus in their bloodstream.

Intermittent virus production from reactivation of a small proportion of latently infected CD4+ T cells (rather than low levels of ongoing replication) is thought to drive viral rebound detected in blood of well-suppressed patients on treatment6-8.

As earlier studies only examined viral sequences derived from the blood of patients who continued to suppress viral replication in that anatomic compartment11, the conclusions are not necessarily generalizable to other compartments in the body, particularly to lymphoid tissue where the frequency of infection per cell is mostly higher12 and the intracellular drug concentrations are much lower than in blood13.

Our sampling approach differs fundamentally from those of previous studies14-16, which do not address evolutionary dynamics within lymphoid tissue, and better suits investigation of the dynamic nature of the viral reservoir during treatment with potent antiretroviral drugs.

Previous work established that viral sequences contemporaneously sampled from lymphoid tissue in different locations are genetically homogeneous17, consistent with CD4+ T cell homing and trafficking18.

Consistent with ongoing replication rather than sampling of different virus populations in lymph nodes, viral sequences contemporaneously sampled from lymphoid tissue and blood showed a similar degree of divergence.

We restricted the test to internal branches, which capture at least one and likely multiple rounds of virus replication, to mitigate the biasing effects of neutral or deleterious mutations on the ratio of nonsynonymous-to-synonymous substitution rates (ω) estimates where selection has not yet fully filtered such population level variation25,26.

Except for one study subject (1679), where a small proportion of sites (0.3%) were under strong diversifying positive selection along internal tree branches (likelihood ratio test, P~10−6), we found scarce evidence to suggest the virus is evolving in response to strong selective forces.

To infer evolutionary patterns and population dynamic processes from the time- structured sequence data, we used a Bayesian statistical framework that estimates the substitution rate, divergence time, and demographic history of the sampled viral lineages to structure-rooted, time-resolved phylogenies27,28 (see Methods).

Our results, which reconstruct the dynamics of HIV-1 spread within the body, imply that in patients with no detectable viral RNA in plasma, the virus reservoir is constantly replenished by low-level virus replication in lymphoid tissue.

A small number of HIV-1 sequences isolated at consecutive time points that persisted without evidence of genetic change might be due to long-lived central memory cells, a fraction of which may have reverted to a resting state, or latently infected transitional memory cells that persist by clonal expansions (driven by homeostatic proliferation) or survivorship for long-lived infected CD4+ T cells that contain replication- competent virus8,15,22,31-34.

Regardless of the different mechanisms for self-renewal and/or persistence by which some of these quite similar latent or defective viral lineages may have persisted, these quiescent viruses differ from others that have evolved and trafficked between compartments.

The temporally and compartmentally sampled data show that viral lineages continue to diverge in well-suppressed patients and help explain the persistence of infectious viral reservoirs with scant decay of the virus pool35.
This study reveals how dynamic and spatial processes work together to permit HIV-1 to persist within the infected host and avoid development of resistance despite antiretroviral therapy.

We estimated trees on viral sequence sets from which gaps in the alignment were removed and considered as missing data for the reason that maximum-likelihood tree error may increase with inclusion of unreliable sites.

We tested whether or not a proportion of sites along internal branches of the intra-host viral phylogeny have been subject to episodic selection (ω > 1)24, restricting the test to internal branches to lessen the biasing effects of neutral or deleterious mutations on ω estimates48,49 and serve as a proxy for population level selection25,26.

We argue that, typically, fully drug resistant mutants of this sort neither exist in the viral population of patients before treatment, nor arise through random mutation during the course of antiretroviral therapy (see Supplementary Information and Supplementary Table 2).

Intranasal inoculation of SARS-CoV-2 in K18-hACE2 mice results in high levels of viral infection in lungs with spread to other organs.
A decline in pulmonary function occurs 4 days after peak viral titer and correlates with infiltration of monocytes, neutrophils, and activated T cells.

Infection was accompanied by declines in multiple parameters of pulmonary function, substantial cellular infiltrates in the lung composed of monocytes, neutrophils, and activated T cells, high levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in lung homogenates, and severe interstitial and consolidative pneumonia.

As no infectious virus and only low levels of viral RNA were detected in the brain of the majority (60%) of animals, the observed clinical disease is more consistent with lung and not brain infection.

The measurements of mechanical properties of the respiratory system suggest that SARS-CoV-2 infection in K18-hACE2 mice predominantly causes disease in the alveoli and lung parenchyma, and not in the conducting airways, which is consistent with both our histopathological analysis in mice and measurements of pulmonary function in humans with viral pneumonia and respiratory failure including COVID-1916.

To evaluate the composition of the immune cell response in SARS-CoV-2-infected K18-hACE2 mice, we performed flow cytometric analysis on lung homogenates and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid at three time points after intranasal virus inoculation (Fig 4a–b, Extended Data Fig 3a) Consistent with our histopathological analysis, numbers of CD45+ immune cells trended higher in the BAL beginning at 2 dpi and in the lung at 4 dpi, although these differences did not attain statistical significance.
The cellular infiltrates at 4 and 7 dpi in the lung were composed principally of myeloid cell subsets including Ly6G+ neutrophils, Ly6C+ monocytes, and CD11b+CD11c+ dendritic cells.

Accumulation of monocytes in the BAL fluid coincided with a decrease in the number of tissue-resident alveolar macrophages, an observation consistent with scRNA-seq analysis of BAL fluid of patients with severe COVID-19 disease18,19.

By 7 dpi, we also observed an increase in several lymphoid cell subsets in the lung including NK1.1+ natural killer cells, γδ CD3+ T cells, CD3+CD4+ T cells, CD3+CD8+ T cells, and activated CD44+CD3+CD8+ T cells (Fig 4a).

Brain tissues of K18-hACE2 mice with minimal or no detectable SARS-CoV-2 infection appeared normal without evidence of microglial activation or inflammation, whereas the one brain recovered with a high level of infection at 7 dpi showed inflamed meningeal vessels with extravasation of immune cells (e.g., neutrophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes) into the brain parenchyma, inflammation of the subarachnoid space and underlying parenchyma including microglial activation (Extended Data Fig 2b).

Beginning at 4 days post-infection (dpi), K18-hACE2 mice demonstrated marked weight loss, and by 7 dpi most animals had lost approximately 25% of their body weight (Fig 1a), with many becoming moribund.

At 2 dpi, we observed accumulation of immune cells confined predominantly to perivascular sites.
By 4 dpi, these immune cell infiltrates involved a greater area of the lung with focal collections into adjacent alveolar spaces with alveolar wall thickening.
